subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ACCREDITATION OF LATVIAN AND ESTONIAN HONORARY CONSULS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on the occasion of the 11th Baltic evening, recently sponsored by the Baltic Federation in Canada representing the Estonian Central Council in Canada, the Latvian National Federation in Canada, and the Lithuanian Canadian community, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) brought to the attention of the House, under the provisions of Standing Order 21, certain irregularities in dealing with the accreditation of Baltic Consuls by the Government of Canada.
These Baltic Federations represent loyal Canadians who have selected Canada as the land of their destiny. They have made significant contributions to the arts and culture of this country. They have added to the ranks of our professionals in the fields of engineering and medicine. They are loyal citizens, conscious of their responsibility to this country, and have responded to this responsibility with dedication and zeal.
I would like to add my concern that two members of the Baltic Federation, the Latvians and the Estonians, unlike the Lithuanians, have not been accorded an accredited status for their consuls. Giving accredited status to these Consuls would show Canada's appreciation for the role that the peoples of Baltic origin have played and are playing in the development and promotion of the homeland of their choice, Canada, and it would serve as a useful link with citizens in the land of their origin. I therefore would urge the Government to grant accredited status to a Latvian and Estonian Consul.

subsubtopic: ENDORSEMENT OF FORMER MINISTER'S POLICIES BY ALASTAIR GILLESPIE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on April 21, 1982, there was a meeting in Toronto organized by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), the then Minister of Finance, and three Toronto Ministers. The invited guests were 14 businessmen. The Globe and Mail of April 22,
1982, reported that 13 out of the 14 businessmen rejected the MacEachen theory about wage and price controls.
Alastair Gillespie was one of the 14 businessmen who claimed to The Globe and Mail that Mr. MacEachen received a "resounding vote of confidence" from the businessmen. The Globe and Mail of April 24, 1982, reported that Robert Owen, President of the Toronto Real Estate Board, "... disagreed with Alastair Gillespie . . . that the businessmen gave Mr. MacEachen a resounding vote of confidence." The Globe and Mail of May 13, 1982, reported that John S. Dewar, Chairman of Union Carbide, denied that there was support for Mr. MacEachen's policies at that meeting. The Globe and Mail of July 10, 1982, reported that only one favoured MacEachen's policies.
Under the circumstances, Madam Speaker, one can easily ask was the Gillespie endorsement of the Minister's economic policies, as well as his false claim of universal endorsement by businessmen, a quid pro quo for the Deputy Prime Minister's endorsement of Mr. Gillespie's lucrative participation in the Scotia Coal Synfuels project? And is there any connection between Mr. Gillespie's enthusiasm for the Minister's ill-fated economic policies and the subsequent decision by the Government to proceed with further re-evaluation of financing of the Gillespie consortium?

subsubtopic: CALL FOR TAX RELIEF
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my opinion the handicapped are ill treated. For the past two years 1 have made numerous representations to the Government on behalf of the disabled persons of Canada. Today I make one further public representation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), asking him to review the position of the disabled with regard to the Income Tax Act. In particular, I would like the Government to include provisions in the next budget which would offset the additional costs incurred by the working disabled by such things as equipment and clothing, and transportation to unserviced industrialized areas.
I am aware that recommendation 46 of "Obstacles" is currently under consideration. I urge the Government to include this recommendation in the next budget because I believe that it will improve the tenuous position of the partially disabled. The present legislation is so narrow in its interpretation that it openly discriminates against handicapped people, many of whom are members of the work force. These people contribute to society through their taxes and are not dependent on society to keep them.
We have a chance to atone for our past neglect. We have a chance in the next budget to lighten the daily burden carried by the disabled. I, therefore, encourage the Minister of Finance to put forth some practical legislation to overcome the key obstacles faced by disabled persons.

AECL's Chalk River laboratory is buying weapons-grade-enriched uranium from the U.S. Department of Energy's nuclear weapons refinery at Oak Ridge, Tennessee. When Chalk River is finished with this enriched fuel, it is sold and delivered to the Savannah River weapons reprocessing plant in South Carolina. Three U.S. States and approximately 40 U.S. municipalities have passed regulations to prevent AECL from shipping this irradiated poison through their areas, because a ten-second direct exposure to this material is lethal. Rather than listening to these people, AECL's shipper is fighting these regulations in the U.S. courts so that we can continue to sell Canadian uranium to the U.S. weapons program.

subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER FROM UNITED STATES SOURCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in February of 1980, when he was the then Leader of the Opposition, undertook to urge the United States authorities to stop the pollution of the Niagara River. The Canada/U.S. task force recently reported that they had identified 300 polluters and that the international quality standards of the Great Lakes were being violated. Various substances have been found in the drinking water on which we have very little information.
The long-term solution to this environmental problem hinges on the outcome of a lawsuit initiated against Hooker Chemical with respect to the Love Canal. Environment Canada and this Government have refused to intervene in those court proceedings.
The presence of dioxin, the deadliest chemical known to man, has been detected for the first time in untreated lake water samples. That finding should finally provide the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) and the Prime Minister with sufficient cause to take more positive action now to protect the water supply of four million Canadians. Failure to do so simply leaves those Canadians as subjects of chemical experimentation. Can anything be more irresponsible?

speechtext:

I am writing to bring to your attention the enclosed guidelines which establish the conflict of interest regime for Ministers and set the standards of conduct expected of them.
In the House on Monday the Deputy Prime Minister stated that the conflict rules as outlined by the Prime Minister "are only self-enforcing guidelines", that is, subject only to the conscience of the individual Minister. In any official dealings with former office holders, Ministers must ensure that they do not provide grounds or the appearance of grounds for allegations of improper influence, privileged access or preferential treatment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I read the Hansard of the past two days attentively. It would seem to me that the discussion permitted the Deputy Prime Minister to make the points which I was attempting to make last week in other words, that there was no improper influence, that there was no privileged access, and that there was no preferential treatment.
How could there be privileged access when we know that under this energy agreement with the Province of Nova Scotia there have been some 13 enterprises, some receiving as much as $3 million, which have proceeded under this? There was no preferential access. This was one of 13 which had access to the policy of the Government, and which was carrying out the intention of the legislation and the policy.
As a matter of fact, how could we claim improper access, privileged access, when the former Minister, Mr. Gillespie, did not even see the Minister? He was not seeking that kind of privileged access. He was going down at the official level.
How can we claim that there was improper influence when, as the Deputy Prime Minister pointed out, the funds were under the control of the Government of Nova Scotia? The agreement said so quite clearly: "The money shall become the public money of the Province of Nova Scotia". That is written in the agreement between Nova Scotia and the Government of Canada. The $9.3 million, I think, is transferred to the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the Government of Nova Scotia. How can we claim there was improper influence?
As to the third element of the guidelines, preferential treatment, I think the facts have shown that, far from giving preferential treatment to the former Minister, there was, in a sense, discrimination against him because there was a reopening of the Treasury Board submission to ensure that none of the money which had been transferred from the Government of Canada to the Government of Nova Scotia would be available or payable to the former Minister.
So, in a sense, a special effort was made by the Department to ensure that there be no privileged treatment and no preferential treatment. It seems to me, Madam Speaker, that that is the substance of the matter.
Has there been some scandalous misconduct or not? I repeat the question asked by the Deputy Prime Minister yesterday and the day before: has there been in substance anything done which a current Minister should not do and should not allow? My answers are no, Madam Speaker.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
that Bill C-346, an Act to amend the Public Service Employment Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act (political rights), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

February 23, 1983
Public Service
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my Bill is to give political rights to Government workers. Under present legislation hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers are denied rights which other Canadians have. Basically those rights concern the right to participate and work in general elections at the provincial or federal level on their own time. There are also restrictions on whether or not they are able to run in general elections. We in the New Democratic Party believe that those restrictions speak against the fundamental rights of all Canadians.
Since I wrote this Bill and had it introduced in the House of Commons for first reading, we have passed the new Canadian Constitution. I would like to read the relevant sections of the Constitution dealing with fundamental freedoms:
Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:
(a)	freedom of conscience and religion;
(b)	freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of
the press and other media of communication;
(c)	freedom of peaceful assembly; and
(d)	freedom of association.
Then I should like to refer to Section 32, entitled "Application of Charter", wherein it reads:
This Charter applies
(a) to the Parliament and the Government of Canada in respect of all matters
within the authority of Parliament-
I hope the Official Opposition and the Government do not talk this Bill out, and that indeed we will refer it to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates for discussion, for study and for presentation by interested groups, so that we can meet the obligations of the new Constitution of Canada. It is essential that we in the House support the Constitution we passed just over a year ago. It is essential that we recognize workers in the public sector should have the same rights as those in the private sector.
This is not a new concept; it is already accepted by the Province of Manitoba. It has been legal there, not only as a result of its introduction by the Schreyer administration, but it was not changed by the Conservative Government of Premier Lyon. It has been accepted and has worked for a number of years in one Province of this land. I urge Members on all sides of the House to give Government workers these democratic rights. Also I urge the Government not to be dragged into the courts, shouting and screaming against giving Government workers these rights.
We do not want a situation where again the Government is afraid to promote rights or to give leadership in granting rights, and is instead in the position of being forced into granting rights to its employees.
I should like to refer to some correspondence which I have in my possession. The first letter was directed to my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), from the former Secretary of State, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan), and was written on May 27, 1982. In part it reads:
It is not the Government's intention at the present time to amend the Public Service Employment Act in such a way that public servants would be allowed to engage in political activities.
The Government is saying that it will not grant these rights even after the passing of the new Canadian Constitution. Following that, on June 25, 1982 the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mr. Kelly), when he was Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board, spoke at a gathering of the National Union of Provincial Government Employees. I will not quote him directly but I will refer to some coverage of that particular meeting wherein it was reported:
Because there are so many public employees and the role of Government has become so pervasive in our society, Kelly suggested, there may be better arguments for maintaining restrictions than easing them.
That was very interesting, because three days later the Government introduced its budget which brought in the six and five legislation. That legislation affected hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers. It restricted their salaries and their pensions. Those workers who were denied their bargaining rights were also denied protection which was available to other workers in the land. Basically they are being told that they have no political right to work for another political Party. They are being told that they cannot write letters on behalf of political Parties which support their position and that they cannot canvass for political candidates who support their position. This present arrangement of the Government of Canada is a real infringement upon the freedom of expression and freedom of association of these employees.
Also I should like to refer to a number of letters on this particular issue which I have received over the years. I have taken the necessary liberty of removing the names and addresses of the people who wrote these letters because it could cost them their jobs. The first letter reads:
I would like to clarify and explain my own situation which should describe more fully my own special interest in this change.
I am currently president of a federal riding association and am also an employee of the federal Government falling under the rules of this ridiculous piece of legislation known as the Public Service Employment Act. I plan on offering as a candidate whenever Pierre chooses to call an election; however, it would be nice to be able to start assuming a public profile before this without fear of losing my job.
I am active in my union and in the party but have so far resisted the urge to publicly criticize the Government on anything other than Public Service issues.
That is one restriction. A government worker who wishes to seek election has to stay in the closet because of the legislation of this land.

These relate specifically to the interpretation of Sec. 32 1(a) of the Public Service Act.
I was informed by my superior of Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada that as a federal employee I was in violation of the aforementioned Act and would now be subject to disciplinary action culminating in dismissal.
In a desperate effort to maintain my livelihood I have therefore with a great deal of chagrin submitted my resignation to the NDP-Quebec Executive.
There are people who have genuine political beliefs. I am sure that letters like these could be written to Conservative and Liberal Members of Parliament. These are people who have a genuine interest and like to work in the political process. They are people who have a genuine interest and would like to run as candidates and work during elections, but the present laws of this land prevent that. People deserve better. There are people who feel threatened under the existing legislation of this land.
Let me read from an article that appeared in the Ottawa Journal on Wednesday, February 6, 1980 during the last federal election. It was a charge made against the Public Service Commission. The article referred to Bill Doherty, Vice-President of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, and it reads:
The commission's threat, Doherty charged yesterday, is contained in its note that the lack of "firm precedents" as to what constitutes illegal political activity means "public servants are advised to exercise care so as not to engage in activities which might be construed as contravening the act."
If I were a Government worker and I received a letter similar to the one I have just quoted, I would be afraid to do anything in a federal election. That letter from the Chairman of the Public Service Alliance of Canada says the law is unclear, that you have to be careful and watch out because you do not know what will happen to you if you take part in a federal election.

The Ottawa Citizen in an editorial entitled "Restore a basic right" on February 7, 1980 remarked on the issue. A paragraph from that editorial is quite informative. It reads:
The law is made all the more ridiculous by the patronage system. The Government asks its secretaries to be non-partisan but it appoints former Cabinet Ministers to head up Government agencies. Who is more sensitive to political pressure? Or, men who have served a political party for years are suddenly appointed to the bench and assumed to be independent and unbiased.
Again, we have an example where some people who have been political all their life are deemed to be unbiased. Yet some worker, it may be someone picking up garbage, it may be someone working in an airport or someone performing secretarial duties in one of the offices across this land, is denied political rights in this country. These are not just idle concerns. As we look through the history of this country, we see how this legislation has been enforced.
In 1978, a Mr. Garth Brewer of Woodstock, New Brunswick, received a letter from the Government of Canada. It read:
As you have already been informed, the Public Service Commissioners are unable to grant your request for leave of absence without pay under the terms of the Public Service Employment Act.
The Commission has carefully reviewed the responsibilities which devolve upon you as a Customs Inspector. For reasons listed in the attached record of your meeting with the Commissioners, on October 6, 1978, the Commission regretfully cannot conclude that your duties are such that your usefulness to the Public Service, were you to return to your position after engaging in political activities, would not be impaired.
The Public Service Commission of Canada said that a customs inspector may not run for election that the job is so politically sensitive that the worker may not engage in an election campaign as a candidate. Mr. Brewer did run. He was fired. Later on he was reinstated.
During the 1980 federal election Mr. Brewer wrote a letter to the Woodstock Bugle. One of the phrases in the letter reads:
Keep Petro-Canada, Sell Clark.

One of my concerns about the present law is that it creates a hardship for people who wish to become candidates if nominations are called early. 1 can give an example of a person who faced this situation in Manitoba. I can mention her name now because she no longer works for the Government of Canada. She was a Government employee named Lee Monk who was forced to resign after she received an NDP nomination. This nomination was given about six months prior to the actual election being called and it was 17 months prior to an election having to take place. She lost her income for that period of time. If it was not for the fact that her husband was working she could not have sought election. Therefore, there is discrimination against those without independent income and those with lower income. That is one reason the law should be changed.
I believe the basic reason for changing the law, if we believe in a truly democratic society that all Canadians deserve the same rights and that our elections are an important part of the democratic process, is that we should ensure that this group- 500,000 Canadians-are not restricted and prevented from exercising those democratic rights. They should not have to live in fear of persecution and prosecution. I have cited one example of this. They should be able to depend on the Parliament of Canada to give them those rights that are outlined in our Charter. They should expect the Parliament of Canada not to slow down that process and to prevent those workers from taking part in federal or provincial elections.
This is a very important matter. I again urge the Opposition and the Government not to talk the Bill out but to act upon it and refer it to the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee so it can study it and listen to those who are concerned with this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), who I know is also interested in this Bill, for letting me speak first. 1 will not occupy too much time so that he and the House can have an opportunity to decide whether this Bill will go to committee.
The purpose of the Bill is set forth in the explanatory notes. It is to provide public servants with the right to engage in political activity and be candidates in federal, provincial and territorial elections. That is the simple statement of the Bill.
I would be inclined to support the Bill, with some reservations, because I think the time has come for some change. I have some questions that I would like to have dealt with in committee which, if answered, may have some bearing with respect to my view of the Bill. Nevertheless, I want to support the Bill so that it will go to committee.
For some time I have asked in the House of Commons that the President of the Treasury Board allow the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee of the House to look into the whole question of political activity by public servants. There are many theories-thousands perhaps-as to what rules should apply. Those theories go all the way from some Members who
believe there should be absolute prohibition of political activity by public servants. Very few Members hold that view. There are some Members who believe that there should be an untrammeled right to political activity. Members holding that view are also few and far between. The extremes of this issue are easy to deal with. It is the views in the middle of that spectrum that are difficult to deal with.
I think it is important that this question be dealt with. The Public Service Commission itself has indicated just what bad shape the law is in at this time.
I am holding a letter dated September 21, 1978, addressed to me from the Chairman of the Public Service Commission. I had written to him on August 25 of that year, asking what constitutes a prescribed political activity for public servants. This is what he said:
As you are aware, the Public Service Commission feels that Parliament should indeed clarify its wishes in this regard in order to enable effective administration of this important section of the Public Service Employment Act. You will recall that we devoted Chapter One of our 1977 Annual Report to a discussion of our concerns about this critical issue.
A part of the problem facing public servants confronted with the question of political activity results from the fact that the current legislative provisions stipulate a general principle (that no employee shall engage in work for, on behalf of or against a candidate for election ... or for, on behalf of or against a political party) and then state that this general principle is not contravened by the simple act of attending a political meeting or contributing money for the funds of a candidate or a political party.
The Chairman of the Public Service Commission goes on to say:
The situation is further complicated by the fact that the Commission has no power to take action in the absence of an allegation being made by a person 'who is or has been a candidate for election'.
He then says:
In the circumstances, it seems to me that Parliament must have intended that the provisions of section 32( 1) and (2) of the Act serve to guide-
We have heard about guidelines today.
-individual public servants in the decisions they have to make when confronted with a concrete situation and have therefore narrowly limited the powers of the Public Service Commission to intervene only in the matter of leave of absence and in those cases where an allegation is made by a person who is or has been a candidate. This would suggest that when a public servant is faced with the question as to whether the action he (she) is about to take or has been asked to take is consistent with section 32 of the Act, that public servant must first ask himself (herself) whether this action could be held to constitute work for, on behalf of or against a candidate for election or a political party and whether or not it falls within the ambit of section 32(2).
In other words, there is no concrete guide; the public servant must ask himself. All of us know that from time to time justice varies with the length of the Chancellor's foot. In other words, there is really no guide for the serving public servant who puts those questions to himself.
I asked the Chairman certain specific questions. The Chairman of the Commission said:
(a)	regarding lawn signs and bumper stickers, we have counselled public servants to adhere strictly to section 32(1) of the Act, pointing out that any action not specifically exempted in section 32(2) could be construed as in violation of the Act.
(b)	regarding the position of a spouse of a public servant, we have taken the stance that this is a matter for parliamentarians or the courts to solve;-

That is a question that does arise in a riding such as mine and others. He also said, with respect to holding membership cards in a political party, that:
-we have said that in our opinion contributing funds to a political party includes the right to hold membership in that party.
That was a letter from the Chairman of the Public Service Commission.

I believe that the general principle which ought to govern is that we ought to be consistent with the maintenance of public order and permit political activity. 1 have often wondered why it might be seen to be improper to show one kind of political act, such as displaying a bumper sticker or a lawn sign, for example, but at the same time, in the quiet of one's room, one can write an application for a membership in a potilical party or write a cheque to a political party. I would have thought that in terms of the conflict which the Statute was meant to attack, however inadequately it does, it would have dealt with the state of mind of the public servant, and the state of mind would be the same whether the Act was public or private. I just raise that for consideration.
It is time that Parliament considered whether or not there is any difference among classes of public servants. We are, for instance, developing a management class within the Public Service of Canada which is outside the bargaining units in the Public Service. These public servants have perhaps somewhat particular duties. People who advise on policy have particular duties in terms of advising the Minister from time to time. A question must at least be raised as to the scope of political activity permitted those people.

We should consider the question. I draw no conclusions. It is worth while investigating. This Statute which has been brought forward by the Hon. Member ought to be studied by a committee of the House for that purpose.
I had the honour to be a member of the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee before the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) was rather unceremoniously removed from his post as Chairman. The Chairman of the Public Service Commission of Canada, in response to questions 1 asked during committee hearings, stated that the time was long overdue for an investigation of that matter. The following witness was the former President of the Treasury Board who is now the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), a super Minister. He, too, said that the time had

come and that he was not opposed. However, like so many things which must be considered, no one moved.
The Government has the right to make references. Perhaps the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee will understand the new mandate given to it by the new Standing Orders of our House and consider it worth while. If it does, then this kind of Bill, which has been put forward by the Hon. Member from his own vantage point, is the kind of Bill which could facilitate a review of that very important matter.
This matter has been continuing much longer than the Neil Fraser case, and I only refer to it in that manner because it is now before the Supreme Court of Canada. That case does raise some great problems and issues, no matter how the Supreme Court of Canada may decide, which could affect the place and position of many public servants beyond the person whose name is on that appeal. I hope the House will agree to send the Bill to committee, as it would be worth while to investigate this whole question.
I must tell the House that there is great interest across the country in this matter, both for and against political rights. It is time that the matter was aired because quite often problems with respect to public servants are neglected rather than reviewed by Parliament. If there is any proof of that, it is the fact that the Finkelman report was worked on by a joint committee, and the findings of that joint committee have gathered dust on the shelves. The only pieces of legislation we have had with respect to public servants have been to cut their wages and pensions. There is more to consideration of public service affairs than that.
I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Lang) is in the House today. It would be good if he were to rise in his place and move a motion, which I would be pleased to second, that at least the subject matter of this Bill go to the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee so that the questions could be resolved.
The Hon. Member who spoke before me inadvertently misled the House with respect to the position of the Ontario Public Service. It is not quite as tough as he said it was. Certainly, Ontario public servants cannot raise money, cannot go door to door and cannot write speeches. They can work in a candidate's office and can have lawn signs on their lawns. I am not arguing that their situation is utopian or perfect by any means, but the problem in the country is that political rights vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, and at least in this jurisdiction we should review them to ensure that they are fair and allow people reasonably to exercise their rights as citizens of the country.
Therefore, I commend the Hon. Member for bringing forth the Bill and I hope its subject matter or the Bill itself can go to committee and we can deal with it.

I should like to quote from an article published by the Ottawa Citizen on October 23, 1979: [English]
The article suggested that the Government amend legislation so federal public servants can work in defence of their country during the Quebec independence referendum next spring.

That was at the time of the Quebec referendum. I quote: [English]
It was suggested that three classes of public servants should be created, with the senior executives being denied all political action, the second group being allowed to campaign only with permission, and the third group having complete freedom.

Mr. Speaker, those comments of course were made following the report submitted by the Special Committee on Personnel Management and the Merit Principle, the so-called D'Avignon Committee, which considered the matter of political involvement where public servants are concerned. True enough, as the previous speaker has remarked, for at least the past four or five years the Government has been reluctant to refer the issue to a Committee. I do not think I am mistaken when I suggest that the Chairman of the Public Service Commission has often called upon Members of Parliament, whenever he appeared before the Committee, to clarify the scope of Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act. I do not think there is any need to repeat the point made by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), which in my view aptly reflects the remarks made by the Chairman of the Public Service Commission.
I would simply like to add that the unions, Mr. Speaker, also share an interest in that review, and that they would appreciate it if the scope of Section 32 were to be clarified. 1 would simply like to support the view of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton to the effect that the matter should be referred to a Committee for consideration, to put an end to the uncertainty that arises whenever an election is called.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I would be making any extraordinary statement if I were to support the comments voiced by the Hon. Member to the effect that here in Ottawa, during
election campaigns, public servants do get involved or would like to get involved in the electoral process, either by having a sign or a poster displayed in their lawn, by wearing a badge or contributing to election funds of any party, but there is that uncertainty concerning the role of public servants. Mr. Speaker, I submit that no Member of Parliament wants or would like to see the impartiality of the Public Service questioned during the electoral process. I do not think such is the issue at hand. However it must be recognized that there is a class of civil servants who do not advise the government on matters of policy. Therefore they should be allowed to take part in the election process. However, I would make an exception in the case of high ranking officials and administrators. As the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, I should like the committee to look into the matter of political activity by public servants. I for one feel that there should be absolute prohibition of any political activity, in their case for the sake of maintaining the integrity of Parliament, so that they may not be seen by the general public as being critical of a government they might have advised.
For this reason, therefore, it is clear to me that senior executives should not be allowed to take part in the election process. Which does not mean that our new Charter of Rights and Freedoms should not be challenged when civil servants or unions feel they are being deprived of their basic rights.
Since Parliament has adopted the Charter, it might be necessary to appeal Section 32 to the courts. I, for one, am not absolutely sure that the Charter of Rights does not apply fully and does not give civil servants complete freedom of speech and the right to get involved in politics. On the other hand, there are things to consider.
The present regime of political activities by public servants is subject to increasing criticism, mainly by Public Service unions and a number of Members of Parliament. I had occasion today to attend a social club in my riding. The speaker was the Chairman of the Public Service Commission. At that time I had no idea 1 would be speaking to this Bill this afternoon. During his remarks to the Richelieu Club of Ottawa, he spoke of political activities by public servants. I understand at this time he is addressing a group of public servants in Touraine on the question.
It is by pure accident that this happens. The main reason is that recently the former Leader of the Official Opposition mentioned that he would like to see some political input into the status of Deputy Ministers. The Ottawa Citizen of January 25, 1983 reported and I quote:
Clark would politicize senior public service posts.
Clark said in an interview he is considering making Ministers' offices more partisan in appointing political Deputy Ministers. Making sure the elected Government gets control of the appointed Government would be his third priority as Prime Minister, the Tory leader said.

Without going into the merits of that argument or the whole question, I hope it will come before the committee and we will be able to discuss it. There are dangerous connotations to the idea of the former Leader of the Opposition. It has prompted certain comments in the Public Service and the Chairman of the Commission felt he had to voice them. He did not say so in his speech, but I read between the lines. 1 would like to share some of the remarks he made today with regard to this question.

This is what Mr. Gallant said: "In my opinion, the role which our Public Service must play as one of the major institutions of our democratic government requires not only that it be impartial, but also that it be seen to be impartial. This is why, in my opinion, it is normal that, on becoming a public servant, we accept not only the advantages this represents, but also all the special responsibilities it entails, including the need to be impartial. While there are obvious differences in the requirement to remain objective in the case of an assistance deputy minister, a laboratory technician and a machine maintenance worker, for instance, it would be difficult and even risky for the Public Service to provide variations in the restrictions of political activity according to the job category and the occupational group."
I shall interrupt my quotation on this point to note that I disagree with the Chairman of the Commission, Mr. Gallant, in this regard. He does not want any variations or exceptions for the various job categories. I shall now continue to quote Mr. Gallant: "As for the suggestion that public employees might participate in partisan political activities on their own time, I believe that this could erode the concept of Public Service impartiality in the eyes of the public, and in this regard, appearances are just as important as the facts themselves."
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the Chairman of the Public Service Commission considered this issue important enough to speak about it twice today, on February 23, once before the Club Richelieu and again this afternoon in Touraine before a group taking part in an orientation program for EX-4's and EX-5's.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to use up all the time at our disposal because I would like this bill to be referred to a committee for study and examination. I believe that the government should resume examination in the House of this very important question, namely section 32 of the PSEA (Public Service Employment Act) and the way it affects public servants, and that it should provide a clear explanation of this provision so that we may all know where public servants stand as far as their political

Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) that if the Government is not prepared to accept the Bill, that it not now be read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to the appropriate standing committee of this House. I do so because I believe the fears of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton and the Hon. Member who just spoke are totally unfounded. Even in the case of senior executive advisers to Government, 99 per cent of the time they will not get involved with politics. If they did and if they could not agree with their Minister, they would invariably resign from their job or be fired. That has always been the case.
The experience of those having to apply for leave of absence, whether it be from a private corporation or Government, to run as a candidate or work in an election at all three levels, municipal, provincial and federal, over the last number of years has been generally good. It is improving. The main anachronisms and nineteenth century state of mind remain only in federal legislation and that of a few Provinces.
In my Province people have run in municipal, provincial and federal elections for all parties-I repeat, all political parties- even though they have been in the employ of the provincial Government, a branch, agency or Crown corporation. Following their leave of absence, they returned to their position. They did not allow their political beliefs to interfere with their duties when they were on duty. They carried on with their duties conscientiously.
That was my experience also, Mr. Speaker, when I was an employee of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When I was there from 8.30 to 5.30 I conducted the business of the Company according to the rules and the policies of the Company. When I was a candidate for public office and criticized the Company's policies after my hours of duty, and when I was on leave of absence without pay, at no time did the Company ever try to penalize me when I returned to work. When my leave of absence expired, I returned to my duties and carried them out conscientiously. My efforts to be elected to public office while I was an employee in no way either impinged upon the Company or harmed my usefulness to them in terms of what I knew about working for a railroad. I believe a lot of these fears are totally unfounded in actual experience and practice. There is little or nothing to fear from providing full political rights to public servants at all levels of Government.

Fine. Mr. Speaker, I believe in years to come, looking back, there are going to be a lot of people wondering why this legislation or something similar to it was not in fact passed. I believe they will look back and ask what all the concern was about, all this fear. We recognize now that some people who are public servants are participating in the political process in one way or another. Sometimes, as many of us politicians know, they make a significant contribution to a particular campaign. But we must always wonder if they are not really going counter to the conditions under which they were hired as public servants. I am quite sure that any public servant spoken to by Hon. Members of this House is quite content and satisfied that he or she can perform service as a professional in the Public Service in those circumstances, be it at the federal or the provincial level. These public servants do not feel inhibited in any way in carrying out their responsibilities in a particular Department.
The very careful presentation of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the considered opinions of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) are understandable because they have probably carried out more research in this particular field than many Hon. Members of Parliament, primarily, of course, because they have a large majority of public servants in their ridings. They are endeavouring to establish not only what would be fair for the Public Service, but also how the general public would perceive involvement of a public servant in a political campaign.
I believe the time is almost ideal to make the kind of changes which this Bill envisages, because in effect we are almost between elections. I believe immediately after an election, when you have won an election, you are really not particularly concerned that someone from the Public Service participated in the campaign, and participated against you. By the same token, if there is a very close race, someone who has lost an election may very well want to take revenge, if you will, or make a particular move which would discredit the public servant, and might, in the final analysis, result in discipline or, for that matter, that particular public servant might lose his or her job. For that reason, the Public Service Commission, I would suggest Hon. Members of this House, and the public at large are endeavouring to struggle with two rights.
What is in the public interest? We heard from the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier who quoted Mr. Gallant, President of the Public Service Commission. He wants to see impartiality throughout. I agree with the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier; 1 believe that is pushing it a little too far. I do not believe we need to be concerned about someone who is doing some filing, clerical work or typing manuscripts or reports, someone who is not, in effect, giving policy advice in a particular Department. I believe you can go a long way up the ladder before that kind of involvement or participation would be of any concern.
I share the hesitation of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton, who accepts this Bill with certain reservations, and that is with respect to the management class, because here is an area where people in that particular category have to draft papers on behalf of a Minister or a Department on how to deal with a particular problem or a particular subject matter. These
individuals are clearly the jumping-off place, or the foundation, if you will, of maybe a particular piece of legislation, or maybe only a policy, but in either event they are in a position to have an influence. I believe the Department, the Minister involved, and certainly Parliament, would want to have the feeling that this individual was acting in a professional capacity, giving his or her best efforts to that particular project. But they might feel that the general public, knowing that the individual who prepared this document was in fact campaigning of behalf of an Opposition Member in the House of Commons or in the legislature, might wonder how objective that person could be. The individual might be a true professional, of which I feel there is an abundance in the federal Public Service. Certainly that has been my experience over the 15 years I have been here. The individual might be a wonderful professional public servant, but because of his or her participation in an election campaign, helping one of the Opposition Parties, would his or her particular representation or presentation not be suspect in that it might very well have been influenced by the Opposition Party in the House, or by the political philosophy of an Opposition Party? So without appropriate guidelines that public servant is in a very difficult spot.
There are guidelines at the present time, and I believe Section 32 has been quoted, but it does allow a lot of discretion to a public servant in that particular category. I heard a small interjections from across the way. They will have to be the authors of their own decision as to whether or not they are in violation of the guidelines. If we just had an out-and-out right, a civil liberty, if you will, a right of a public servant to participate in the political process, there would not be any difficulty and we might very well not need any legislation. But obviously, what we have here is a situation where you have two rights. There is the freedom of an individual to have a political opinion and to help a particular Party. But there is also the public interest, where the public must have the feeling and the assurance that this individual public servant is acting in a professional capacity and that the opinions expressed are professional opinions and not the opinions of a particular Party which he or she may have supported.
What I am emphasizing here, Mr. Speaker, is that we have the public interest versus a basis democratic right, and it is a legitimate debate. I am not certain that the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates is the appropriate forum. Everyone seems to want to deal with this. Even the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton quoted a letter, which is already five years old, where at that time the President of the Public Service Commission thought it was a good idea to deal with this. Then there was a quote from a former President of the Treasury Board to the effect that he thought it was a good idea that it be dealt with.
Mr. Speaker, it strikes me more and more like heaven. Everyone wants to go, but not necessarily right now. That
February 23, 1983

seems to be the way this particular policy is being handled, and I think that is to the detriment, frankly, of the Public Service. I do not think that the general public needs to feel fearful. 1 feel that managers and people at that particular level of the Civil Service should not be participating in the political process.
I wonder if we should not try out on an experimental basis the removal of many of these guidelines and say that people can run as candidates-if they run as candidates I think we would require them to get a leave of absence-but if they want to help a particular candidate, let that individual do so. I think that the practical experience that was referred to by the Member from Regina would probably come to the fore. We would find that a large number of them would not participate in any event, but it would allow the people who want to participate to do so. To what extent would they feel inhibited in doing their work? I think they would not feel that way at all, but it would indicate to the more wary public servants that they could participate in this. Otherwise, what we are going to have is that only those who are prepared to take a chance and to stick their necks out will participate and will run the risk of losing their jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I did not realize that the time had moved on so quickly. I thought there was another Member rising to speak, but I understand my time is up. I think it is an interesting subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

I wonder if I might indicate to the House that the next order of business would be a Bill put by the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), and I understand that he seeks the floor on a point of order to deal with that matter.
When the House has heard the Hon. Member, perhaps the Chair would recognize the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) with respect to the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mr. Gourd).
As the House has heard, the Parliamentary Secretary has indicated that that Member has been unavoidably detained.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity to discuss with my Party's House Leader, with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard), the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) and with the New Democratic Party the fact that perhaps this Bill should not be dealt with today and, with unanimous consent, could be put over until next Wednesday as some discussions within the Department of Finance might allow this Bill to have a longer
Public Service
life than most Private Members' Bills. I would be quite happy to have this happen, with unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that request is agreeable to this side of the House.

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, that request is also agreeable to us.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext: Does the House accept by unanimous consent the proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton, and agreed to by other spokesmen, that the matter be withdrawn today and that it retain its place on the Order Paper for this day next week. Is there unanimous consent?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think under the circumstances we might have agreement that we now see the clock as reading six o'clock.

speechtext: Agreed.

Considering that we do have some one and a half hours before the normal adjournment hour, I wonder whether, by unanimous consent, the House might agree to give further consideration-it seemed to have a great deal of support in terms of its substance-to Bill C-46 which stands in the name of my

February 23, 1983
Public Service
colleague, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). Could we seek unanimous consent?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext:

If he were putting a motion under Standing Order 8(4)(a) then, as he is aware, it would require 25 Members standing in their place to deny that.
In the alternative, he may be seeking unanimous consent to extend the debate on the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Churchill. It is my impression that that cannot be done, given the fact that that hour has now expired. I think that a motion made after the time has expired would probably not be in order, but if the Hon. Member for Kootenay West wishes to persist, I will seek consultation as to whether or not that is possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ENGAGING IN POLITICAL ACTIVITY
speechtext:
